overview: The Komuravelli Mallanna Temple (Sri Mallikarjuna Swamy Devasthanam) is one of the most powerful and culturally vibrant folk-deity temples in Telangana. Located on a low hill (Indrakeeladri) in Komuravelli village, Cherial Mandal, Siddipet district, about 85–95 km from Hyderabad on SH-1 Rajiv Rahadari (Karimnagar–Hyderabad Highway), it is devoted to Lord Mallanna (Mallikarjuna Swamy) — a fierce yet compassionate folk incarnation of Lord Shiva (in 'vigraha rupam' / murti form, with consorts Golla Kethamma and Medalamma), also venerated as Khandoba by Maharashtrian devotees. Unlike traditional Agama-based temples, it embodies Telangana's living folk traditions where devotion is expressed through the Oggu Katha narrative tradition, folk offerings, and vows rather than formal Vedic sevas. The 8-foot clay idol is believed to be ~500 years old. The temple is administered by the Telangana Endowments Department (Dy. Commissioner & Executive Officer). Its signature event is the Komuravelli Mallanna Jathara, one of the biggest folk festivals in Telangana.
summary: The Komuravelli Mallanna Temple (Sri Mallikarjuna Swamy Temple) at Komuravelli, Cherial Mandal, Siddipet district, Telangana, is a major folk-deity shrine dedicated to Lord Mallanna — a Telangana folk form of Lord Shiva (also worshipped as Khandoba) — with consorts Golla Kethamma and Medalamma. Set on Indrakeeladri hill ~85–95 km from Hyderabad, it is rooted in oral tradition and the Oggu Katha folk-narrative form (in Telugu, not Sanskrit) rather than Agama ritual. Worshipped as a guardian deity (Grama Devata) who delivers swift justice and protection, it draws lakhs during the annual Mallanna Jathara (every Sunday from Makara Sankranti to Ugadi) and large crowds every Sunday and Monday. The temple is administered by the Telangana Endowments Department under the Sri Mallikarjuna Swamy Devasthanam Board.

history.content: The temple's history stretches back several centuries and is rooted in oral tradition rather than written records. According to popular tradition, Komaranna, a devotee from the Yadava community, performed deep penance (tapas) for Lord Shiva on this hilltop. Lord Shiva appeared before him as Mallanna, and Komaranna installed the divine 8-foot clay idol on the hill, establishing the shrine. A separate popular legend holds that Lord Mallikarjuna appeared in a dream to a shepherd and told him he was enshrined on Indrakeeladri hill in 'Putta Matti' (soft earth) to fulfill devotees' desires. The current clay idol is believed to be ~500 years old. Worship of Mallanna originally flourished among shepherds, farmers and warriors, and over time the site transformed into a major pilgrimage centre attracting devotees from across Telangana. As the rush of devotees increased, the temple committee (and later the Endowments Department) renovated the temple complex, built mandapams, choultries, rest rooms, water facilities, and the 200+ room accommodation block. The Mallanna story has no written script — it is preserved and sung in the Oggu Katha folk-narrative tradition by the Oggu community.

sthala_puranam: Lord Mallanna, the Telangana folk-form of Lord Shiva, is revered as a guardian deity (Grama Devata) of villages, livestock and the rural poor. According to popular tradition, Komaranna of the Yadava community performed intense penance on Indrakeeladri hill, and Lord Shiva appeared before him as Mallanna. Komaranna installed the 8-foot clay idol, which remains the presiding deity. Mallanna's story — unwritten and transmitted orally — is performed in the Oggu Katha by hereditary singer-storytellers (the Oggu community), who narrate his exploits and his marriage to the goddess Medalamma after overcoming the conditions set by her brothers. Devotees believe Mallanna hears prayers directly and delivers immediate justice, mediating land, legal and family conflicts.
religious_significance: Mallanna is at the heart of Telangana's folk devotion, embodying faith, social justice and community bonding that bridges castes and classes. He is seen as a champion of justice and truth, a mediator for land, legal and family conflicts, a protector of villages and livestock, and a vanquisher of fear, evil spirits and negative energies. Devotees regard him as a 'living god' who hears prayers directly without intermediaries. He is especially popular among the Kuruma, Mudhiraj, Yadava and other BC communities. The temple is one of the prominent Shiva shrines in northern Telangana, alongside Vemulawada (Rajarajeshwara) and Kaleshwaram (Mukteshwara).
spiritual_significance: The temple is believed to be a sacred spot for instant justice and divine protection. Devotees come seeking help with health issues, court cases, family concerns and land disputes. Unlike classical Agama temples, worship here is heartfelt, emotional and woven into everyday rural life, expressed through folk offerings and vows rather than formal paid rituals. All mantras are chanted in Telugu (not Sanskrit) — a distinctive inclusive tradition that sets this temple apart from most major Indian shrines.

architecture: The temple is built in a simple folk-temple style (no towering gopurams) and is located in a cave on the Indrakeeladri hillock, reached by a short climb of about 100 steps. The main sanctum houses Lord Mallanna in a humble folk style as a seated 8-foot clay murti in 'vigraha rupam' (statue form) rather than the more common 'linga rupam'. The complex includes a Medalamma (consort) sannidhi, subsidiary shrines for Ganesha, Nandi and the Navagrahas (on an elevated platform), and a Veera Bhadra cave temple (with a sacred Shiva Linga and Nandi) reached by climbing a few more steps. There are separate passages for entrance and exit from the cave temple. The main entrance tower, compound wall, Mukhamantapa and cottages are painted in yellow to mark them as temple property. The complex has a spacious open courtyard for large gatherings, and ~200 rooms for devotees' accommodation managed by the Devasthanam Board.

timing_conflict_note: Significant source conflict on timings. The most-detailed sources (xploringdestinations.com, templemama.com, multiple Tripadvisor reviews citing the in-situ board) consistently give: temple open 4:30 AM–8:30 PM, with a fixed 12:00 PM–3:00 PM afternoon closure, and general darshan 6:00 AM–12:00 PM and 3:00 PM–7:00 PM. Grokipedia gives 4:00 AM–9:00 PM; a minority of blogs cite 5:00 AM–10:00 PM (extended to near-24x7 during Jathara). The internal ritual schedule (Oggu Prathana, Suprabhatam, Theertha Binde, Darshanam, Nivedana) is also documented. Confirm locally before visiting. Other resolved conflicts: mandal is Cherial Mandal (per official EO address); the Wikipedia text placing it in 'Warangal District' is pre-2022 (Siddipet District is the correct current district).

sevas.name: General Darshan (no formal Agama sevas)
sevas.description: General darshan is free for all. The temple does NOT adhere to formal Agama-based sevas like Abhishekam or Archana; devotion is expressed through folk offerings (coconut-breaking, bonam, kode mokku, patnam rangoli, personal prayers). Reserved sevas and special poojas are available paid at the counter; paid abhishekam slots fill quickly during Jathara. A 'quick darshan' option is also available for a small fee (per Tripadvisor review: 'Devotees can avail quick darshan by paying one hundred rupees each').

festivals.description: The temple's signature annual observance — one of the biggest folk festivals in Telangana. Runs every Sunday from Makara Sankranti (mid-January) to Ugadi (March–April), about 10 Sundays. Features grand bull offerings, vow fulfillment, Oggu Katha performances, folk music, and cultural events. Lakhs of pilgrims congregate on the eve of Makara Sankranti as the Brahmotsavam begins. Largest crowds (50,000–100,000) on the first Sunday after Sankranti and the final Sunday before Ugadi.
All-night vigil; the 'Pedda Patnam' is celebrated on this day, drawing lakhs of pilgrims.
Fire-walking/fire-related observance celebrated on the Sunday falling immediately before Ugadi.
Telugu New Year; marks the closing of the Jathara season.

dress_code: Modest and traditional attire is recommended. Men typically wear a dhoti or simple attire (many remove the shirt at the inner sanctum, per Telugu temple convention); women wear sarees or salwar suits. Footwear is removed at the entrance to the temple grounds.

accommodation.availability: The Komuravelli Devasthanam Board provides ~200+ rooms for devotees on the temple premises, all painted yellow to mark them as registered temple property. Rooms are allotted on a first-come, first-served basis (no online advance booking for rooms); they fill quickly on Mondays, Sundays and during the Jathara season. Most devotees prefer staying in nearby towns like Gajwel or Siddipet, which have a variety of private lodges and hotels.
accommodation.booking_process: No online booking for temple rooms. On arrival, check in at the temple office or accommodation counter for availability. For seva/room reservations, email reservations@komuravelli.org.

best_time_to_visit: Mondays, Sundays and Amavasya days are the principal weekly occasions for Mallanna worship. The Sankranti-to-Ugadi Jathara season is the most vibrant but most crowded. For the Jathara atmosphere without overwhelming crowds, a mid-Jathara Sunday (around the 5th–6th week, ~20,000–30,000 devotees) is the best compromise versus the peak first/last Sundays (50,000–100,000). Avoid peak Jathara days if you dislike crowds. Early weekday mornings are best for peaceful, crowd-free darshan.

About 110 km from Warangal.

All mantras are chanted in Telugu (not Sanskrit), and the Oggu Katha folk-narrative tradition preserves Mallanna's story.

faq.question: What are the visiting hours for Komuravelli Temple?
faq.answer: Per the most detailed sources (xploringdestinations.com, Tripadvisor reviews citing the in-situ board), the temple is open 4:30 AM–8:30 PM with a fixed 12:00 PM–3:00 PM afternoon closure. General darshan is 6:00 AM–12:00 PM and 3:00 PM–7:00 PM. Grokipedia cites 4:00 AM–9:00 PM; some blogs cite 5:00 AM–10:00 PM. Extended / near-24x7 hours during the Jathara season. Confirm locally before visiting.

faq.question: Is there an entry fee to visit Komuravelli Temple?
faq.answer: No. General darshan is completely free; no mandatory ticket is required. A 'quick darshan' option is reportedly available for ₹100 per a single Tripadvisor account — reconfirm on-site.

faq.question: Are there any rituals performed at the temple?
faq.answer: The temple does not follow formal Agama-based rituals. Devotees make folk offerings — breaking coconuts, bonam, kode mokku (bull offering) and patnam rangoli. The daily internal ritual schedule is: Oggu Prathana 4:00–4:30 AM; Suprabhatam Seva 4:30–5:00 AM; Theertha Binde & Rudrabhishekam 5:00–6:00 AM and 7:15 PM; Darshanam 6:00 AM–12:00 PM and 3:00–7:00 PM; Maha Nivedana 12:00 PM; Nivedana 8:00 PM. Reserved sevas, special poojas and annadanam are available online via the Devasthanam Board.

faq.question: When is the best time to visit Komuravelli Mallanna Temple?
faq.answer: Mondays, Sundays, Amavasya days and the Sankranti-to-Ugadi Jathara season are the most auspicious times. A mid-Jathara Sunday offers a vibrant atmosphere with smaller crowds. Early weekday mornings are best for peaceful, crowd-free darshan.

faq.question: How do I reach Komuravelli Temple from Hyderabad?
faq.answer: Take a TSRTC bus from JBS/MGBS to Siddipet or Gajwel (~₹100–200 one-way), then a local bus, auto or shared jeep to Komuravelli village. Special buses run on Mondays, Sundays and during the Jathara. By road it is ~85–95 km (~2–2.5 hours) on SH-1 Rajiv Rahadari.

faq.question: Is there any accommodation near Komuravelli Temple?
faq.answer: Yes — the Komuravelli Devasthanam Board provides ~200+ rooms on the temple premises, painted yellow to mark them as registered temple property. Rooms are first-come, first-served (no online advance booking) and fill quickly on Mondays, Sundays and during the Jathara. Most devotees otherwise prefer staying in nearby Gajwel or Siddipet.

faq.question: What is Komuravelli Jathara?
faq.answer: Komuravelli Jathara is a grand annual folk festival running every Sunday from Makara Sankranti (mid-January) to Ugadi (March–April), drawing lakhs of devotees with bull offerings (kode mokku), vow fulfillment, Oggu Katha performances, fire observances (Agni Gundaalu) and cultural events. The 'Pedda Patnam' on Maha Shivaratri also draws lakhs of pilgrims.

faq.question: Who administers the Komuravelli Mallanna Temple?
faq.answer: The temple is administered by the Sri Mallikarjuna Swamy Devasthanam Board under the Telangana Endowments Department (Dy. Commissioner & Executive Officer). Official contact: phone 08710-226201, general email eo_smdk@yahoo.co.in, reservations email reservations@komuravelli.org, official website srikomuravellimallanna.com.

faq.question: How old is the Mallanna idol?
faq.answer: The 8-foot clay idol of Lord Mallikarjuna Swamy is believed to be about 500 years old, installed by Komaranna of the Yadava community after his penance on Indrakeeladri hill. The deity is 'coloured' (annually re-decorated) once a year.
